rv.q: It’s a fiendishly well-crafted, hilariously smart — or maybe smartly hilarious — song-and-dance extravaganza.
Now The Book of Mormon – aggressively hilarious, blasphemous and almost indecently entertaining – has grabbed a spot in that canon.
“The Book of Mormon” expresses a giddy contempt for that innocence, in one of the most joyously acidic bundles Broadway has unwrapped in years.

It's an often uproarious, spiritually up-tempo satire not just of Mormonism, and not just religion in general, but of (no kidding) Occidental civilization itself, in all its well-intentioned, self-mythologizing, autoerotically entitled glory.
An exhilarating Broadway musical at once revolutionary and classic, funny and obscene, uncompromising in production standards and unafraid of just about anything else.
But gosh darn it if I didn’t feel born again all over again, ready to spread the word about the faith that this show preaches and, more important, practices.
The Book of Mormon is hands down the funniest, most joyfully offensive and breathlessly entertaining new musical in years.
What makes the musical irresistible, however, is its panache in making naughty mockery of a whole string of untouchable subjects, without an ounce of spite.

This raucously funny musical about a pair of mismatched Mormon missionaries is the most joyously acidic Broadway musical in years, a religious satire that's both ruthlessly irreverent and unexpectedly sweet.
“The Book of Mormon” is built for rougher pleasures.
Manages to offend, provoke laughter, trigger eye-rolling, satirize conventions and warm hearts, all at the same time.
The mighty O'Neill himself would have to have given it up for this extraordinarily well-crafted musical assault on all things holy.
The show is blissfully original, irreverent, outspoken and hilarious.
Those exiting prematurely, however, will be missing out on a whole lotta sung, danced and acted glory.

"The Book of Mormon" is a gleefully funny spoof, a blend of the clever and the crass that seldom goes more than 10 seconds without a big laugh. And it's not just about the jokes. They're embedded in a satisfying story, supported by witty, character-relevant songs...one of the most purely enjoyable musicals in years.
The Book of Mormon is both a love letter to and a savage parody of musical theater itself, and it succeeds brilliantly on both counts.
While the plot is somewhat thin and occasionally feels like an overextended sketch, the musical ultimately comes across as fresh, smart and heartfelt.
But after you hold that trial in your head, between laughs, you ultimately end up dismissing the case.

The show--done by the South Park guys with the help of an Avenue Q writer--manages the high-wire feat of spoofing religion, poverty, and Jesus, while throwing in AIDS jokes and songs about closeted Mormons "turning it off"--and virtually everyone leaves happy!

"The sharp-edged book and fun score by Parker, Stone, and Lopez offer a screamingly funny yet sharply insightful full-length take on religion in general and Mormonism in particular. There are also pointed but loving tributes to musical comedy conventions, shockingly vulgar humor, and that rarity on Broadway these days: topical and effective satire.
Like several shows this season, “Book of Mormon” is too long and comes close to wearing out its welcome before redeeming itself with a strong second act.
This is what 21st-century Broadway can be.
The myriad moments that The Book of Mormon is most Broadway, however, are anything but.
Stretched to Broadway length, the duo's patented gags pall: in this surprisingly old-fashioned show
I've rarely laughed so hard, and especially at such seemingly stupid and obviously irreverent jokes.
The Book of Mormon is somehow both jaw-droppingly ill-mannered and adorably innocent, not to mention one of the best new musicals in recent memory.
We can safely say, that with the astonishing “The Book of Mormon” Broadway will never be quite the same again!
The wonderful zest that everybody packs into their performances suggests that they love doing this brilliant show, and who can blame them?
The bottom line is that the show we all hoped would set Broadway on its ear, simply pats it on its back, providing us with generic pastiche comedy and timidly tepid satire.
